provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: The Ministry of Peter (Part 1)
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the events in Acts 8:4-25.
The students should be able to explain the encounter between Peter and Simon.
The students should be able to list lessons from the story of Simon the Magician.
Introduction:
We have learned about the early Church growth after Jesus ascension. Today we will study how Peter continued Jesus ministry through miracles and teaching.
Content:
Peter and John went to Samaria after persecution scattered the believers. They prayed for the people to receive the Holy Spirit. Simon the magician saw this power and offered money to buy it. Peter rebuked him saying money cannot buy Gods gift. Simon asked Peter to pray for him so that nothing bad happens to him. This teaches us that spiritual things cannot be bought with money like buying kerosene at the market.
Class activity:
Students will role-play the scene where Peter meets Simon the magician, showing how Peter rejected Simons offer.
Evaluation questions:
1. Where were Peter and John when they met the Samaritans?
2. What did Simon offer Peter and why?
3. What lesson can we learn from Peters response to Simon?
4. How does this story relate to our Christian life today?
Summary:
The story of Peter and Simon teaches that Gods gifts cannot be bought with money but received through faith and obedience.

topics.title: The Ministry of Peter (Part 2) Dorcas).
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify the two miracles performed by Peter in this passage.
The students should be able to explain how Peter raised Dorcas back to life.
The students should be able to state the results of these miracles.
Introduction:
Last week we studied Peter meeting Simon the magician. Today we will learn about two more miracles Peter performed that showed Gods power working through him.
Content:
Peter traveled to Lydda where he found a man named Aeneas who had been paralyzed for eight years. Peter said Jesus Christ heals you and immediately Aeneas got up. This miracle caused many people in Lydda and Sharon to turn to the Lord. Peter then went to Joppa where a disciple named Dorcas had died. The widows showed Peter the clothes and robes Dorcas had made for them. Peter sent everyone out, knelt down and prayed, then said Tabitha arise. Dorcas opened her eyes and sat up. Many people in Joppa believed in the Lord because of this miracle.
Class activity:
Students will draw pictures of either Aeneas being healed or Dorcas being raised to life, writing a caption explaining what happened.
Evaluation questions:
1. What was wrong with Aeneas and how long had he been like that?
2. What did Peter say to heal Aeneas?
3. What did the widows show Peter before he raised Dorcas?
4. Why did these miracles lead people to believe in the Lord?
Summary:
Peter performed two great miracles in Lydda and Joppa that showed Gods power and led many people to believe in Jesus.

topics.title: The Ministry of Peter (Part 3) - Peter defends his action in Cornelius' house.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to narrate the story of Cornelius conversion.
The students should be able to explain why Peter visited Cornelius.
The students should be able to list the results of Cornelius conversion.
Introduction:
We have studied Peter performing miracles and raising people from death. Today we will learn about how God used Peter to bring the Gospel to non-Jewish people for the first time.
Content:
Cornelius was a Roman army officer who feared God and gave alms generously. An angel told him to send for Peter in Joppa. At the same time, Peter had a vision where God showed him that all foods are clean. The Holy Spirit told Peter to go with the men sent by Cornelius. When Peter arrived at Cornelius house, he preached about Jesus and the Holy Spirit came on all who heard, just as it had on the disciples at Pentecost. Peter baptized Cornelius and his household. Some Jewish Christians criticized Peter for this, but Peter explained that God had given the Holy Spirit to Gentiles too.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to list the events that led to Cornelius conversion in proper order.
Evaluation questions:
1. Who was Cornelius and what was his position?
2. What vision did Peter have before going to Cornelius house?
3. What happened when Peter preached in Cornelius house?
4. How did Peter defend his action to the Jewish Christians?
Summary:
God used Peter to bring the Gospel to Cornelius and other Gentiles, showing that salvation is for all people who believe in Jesus.

topics.title: The Ministry of Peter (Part 4) death of Herod.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe how Peter was imprisoned.
The students should be able to explain how Peter was released from prison.
The students should be able to state what happened to Herod after Peters release.
Introduction:
We have studied Peter performing miracles and bringing the Gospel to Cornelius. Today we will learn about how God miraculously rescued Peter from prison during a difficult time.
Content:
King Herod arrested Peter and put him in prison, planning to kill him after the Passover. The Church prayed earnestly for Peter. One night, an angel appeared, struck Peters chains, led him past the guards and out of the prison. Peter went to the house where the Church was praying and surprised them with his release. Later, Herod wore his royal robes and gave a speech. The people shouted that his voice was like a gods voice. Immediately, an angel struck Herod because he did not give glory to God, and he was eaten by worms and died.
Class activity:
Students will write a short prayer that the Church might have prayed for Peters release, sharing with the class.
Evaluation questions:
1. Why was Peter imprisoned by Herod?
2. How did Peter escape from prison?
3. What happened to Herod after Peters release?
4. What can we learn about prayer from this story?
Summary:
God answered the prayers of the Church and miraculously delivered Peter from prison, while Herod was punished for his pride.

topics.title: Midterm Examination
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate knowledge of Peters ministry through written responses.
The students should be able to recall key events and teachings from the first four weeks.
Introduction:
Today you will have your midterm examination to assess your understanding of the topics we have covered this term.
Content:
The examination will cover all topics from Weeks 1-4, including Peters encounter with Simon, his miracles in Lydda and Joppa, Cornelius conversion, and Peters miraculous escape from prison. Students should review their notes and the Bible passages studied.
Class activity:
The midterm examination will be written in the examination hall under supervised conditions.
Evaluation questions:
The examination will contain multiple choice, short answer and essay questions covering all topics from the first four weeks.
Summary:
This midterm examination will help you demonstrate what you have learned about Peters ministry and the early Church.

topics.title: The Ministry of Apostle Paul (Part 1) Acts 7:57-58; 8:1-3; 9:1-3 - Paul's persecution of the
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to narrate Pauls early life and persecution of the Church.
The students should be able to explain Pauls conversion experience.
The students should be able to list the results of Pauls conversion.
Introduction:
We have studied the ministry of Peter in the early Church. Today we begin studying the life and ministry of Apostle Paul, who was once a fierce persecutor of Christians before becoming a great apostle.
Content:
Paul was born in Tarsus and was a Pharisee who studied under Gamaliel. He was called Saul at first. He witnessed the stoning of Stephen and approved of it. He then began persecuting the Church, going from house to house to arrest both men and women who believed in Jesus. He obtained letters from the high priest to go to Damascus to arrest Christians there. On the road to Damascus, a bright light from heaven flashed around him, and he heard Jesus voice asking why he was persecuting Him. Saul was blind for three days and was healed by Ananias after praying. He then became a follower of Jesus and was baptized, changing his name to Paul.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to create a timeline of Pauls life before and after his conversion.
Evaluation questions:
1. What was Pauls name before his conversion and what was his profession?
2. How did Paul persecute the Church before his conversion?
3. Describe what happened to Paul on the road to Damascus.
4. What changes occurred in Pauls life after his conversion?
Summary:
Paul was a persecutor of the Church who experienced a dramatic conversion and became one of the greatest apostles who spread the Gospel throughout the Roman Empire.

topics.title: Midterm Break
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to rest and prepare for the second half of the term.
The students should be able to revise previously taught topics during the break.
Introduction:
This is a midterm break for students and teachers to rest and recharge after the first half of the term.
Content:
Students should use this break to rest and revise the topics covered in the first four weeks of the term. This will help them better understand the remaining topics on Pauls ministry and Christian unity.
Class activity:
No formal class activities during the midterm break. Students are encouraged to rest and spend time with family.
Evaluation questions:
No formal evaluation during the midterm break.
Summary:
The midterm break provides an opportunity for rest and preparation for the second half of the term.

topics.title: The Ministry of Apostle Paul (Part 2) 13-14 - Paul's first missionary journey.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe Pauls first missionary journey.
The students should be able to list the places Paul visited during his first journey.
The students should be able to explain the results of Pauls first missionary journey.
Introduction:
We studied Pauls conversion last week. Today we will learn about his first missionary journey where he traveled to many places to preach the Gospel.
Content:
Paul and Barnabas were set apart by the Holy Spirit for missionary work. They traveled to Seleucia, then sailed to Salamis in Cyprus. They preached in the synagogues and encountered a sorcerer named Elymas whom Paul blinded. They then sailed to Perga in Pamphylia where John Mark left them. They went to Antioch in Pisidia where they preached in the synagogue. Many Jews and Gentiles believed, but others opposed them. They then went to Iconium, Lystra and Derbe where they also faced opposition and persecution. In Lystra, Paul was stoned and left for dead but recovered. They returned to Antioch, reporting all that God had done through them.
Class activity:
Students will trace Pauls first missionary journey on a map of the ancient world, marking the places he visited.
Evaluation questions:
1. Who joined Paul on his first missionary journey?
2. Name three places Paul visited during his first journey.
3. What happened to Paul in Lystra?
4. What was the result of Pauls first missionary journey?
Summary:
Pauls first missionary journey took him to many cities where he preached the Gospel, faced opposition, and established churches.

topics.title: The Ministry of Apostle Paul (Part 3) right ways of resolving conflicts.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the issues discussed at the Council of Jerusalem.
The students should be able to differentiate between wrong and right ways of resolving conflicts.
The students should be able to apply biblical principles to conflict resolution.
Introduction:
We have studied Pauls missionary journeys. Today we will learn about how the early Church handled conflicts, particularly the important Council of Jerusalem.
Content:
Some Jewish Christians taught that Gentile believers must be circumcised and follow Jewish laws to be saved. Paul and Barnabas disputed this with them. The Church decided to send Paul, Barnabas and others to Jerusalem to discuss this issue with the apostles and elders. After much discussion, Peter explained how God gave the Holy Spirit to Gentiles without requiring circumcision. James then suggested that Gentile believers should avoid certain practices to maintain peace with Jewish believers. The Council agreed, sending a letter to the Gentile churches with these instructions. This shows us how conflicts should be resolved through discussion, prayer, and seeking Gods will, rather than arguing or fighting like children in a school playground.
Class activity:
Students will role-play a scenario where two Christian groups disagree about a practice, showing how to resolve the conflict biblically.
Evaluation questions:
1. What issue was discussed at the Council of Jerusalem?
2. What decision was made regarding Gentile believers?
3. How can we apply the principles of the Council of Jerusalem to conflicts today?
4. What are wrong ways to resolve conflicts according to the Bible?
Summary:
The Council of Jerusalem showed how conflicts in the Church should be resolved through discussion, seeking Gods will, and maintaining unity.

topics.title: Christian Unity and Living Among Non- interdenominational cooperation; Christian giving Christians (Phil. 4:14-20; 2 Cor. 8:3-5; 9:6-15); teachings that
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain biblical teachings on Christian giving.
The students should be able to list ways Christians can promote unity.
The students should be able to describe how Christians should live among non-Christians.
Introduction:
As we conclude this term, we will study important teachings about Christian unity, giving, and living in a multi-religious society like Nigeria.
Content:
The Bible teaches that Christians should give generously and cheerfully, as God loves a cheerful giver. Paul commended the Philippian church for their support of his ministry. Christians should also promote unity across denominations, working together for the common good of the Church and society. In Nigeria, Christians live among people of different faiths, and should demonstrate Christ-like character in their daily lives. They should be respectful, honest, and show love to everyone, even when facing persecution. Christian organizations like the Christian Association of Nigeria work to promote unity and address issues affecting Christians in the country.
Class activity:
Students will write a short paragraph explaining how they can promote Christian unity in their school and community.
Evaluation questions:
1. What does the Bible say about Christian giving?
2. Name two ways Christians can promote unity.
3. How should Christians live among non-Christians in Nigeria?
4. What is the importance of Christian organizations in Nigeria?
Summary:
Christians should live in unity, give generously, and demonstrate Christs character when living among people of different faiths.

topics.title: Revision
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall all topics covered this term.
The students should be able to answer questions about Peters and Pauls ministries.
The students should be able to explain teachings on Christian unity and living.
Introduction:
This week we will revise all topics covered this term to prepare for your final examination.
Content:
We will review Peters ministry, including his miracles, encounter with Simon, Cornelius conversion, and escape from prison. We will also revise Pauls conversion, his missionary journeys, and the Council of Jerusalem. Finally, we will review teachings on Christian unity, giving, and living among non-Christians. Students should ask questions about any topics they find difficult.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to create revision questions for each topic covered this term, then quiz each other.
Evaluation questions:
The revision will include questions covering all topics from Weeks 1-10 to assess understanding and identify areas needing further study.
Summary:
This revision week will help students consolidate their learning and prepare for the final examination.

topics.title: Examination
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate knowledge of all topics covered this term.
The students should be able to apply biblical teachings to various situations.
Introduction:
Today you will have your final examination for this term to assess your understanding of all topics covered.
Content:
The examination will cover all topics from Weeks 1-10, including Peters ministry, Pauls conversion and missionary journeys, the Council of Jerusalem, and teachings on Christian unity and living. Students should review all notes and Bible passages studied.
Class activity:
The final examination will be written in the examination hall under supervised conditions.
Evaluation questions:
The examination will contain multiple choice, short answer and essay questions covering all topics from the term.
Summary:
This final examination will help you demonstrate what you have learned about the early Church and Christian living.

topics.title: Closing
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to reflect on what they have learned this term.
The students should be able to set goals for their spiritual growth.
Introduction:
As we conclude this term, let us reflect on what we have learned and prepare for the next term.
Content:
We have studied the ministries of Peter and Paul, who were key figures in the early Church. We have learned about their challenges, miracles, and teachings that helped establish the Church. We have also learned about Christian unity and living in a multi-faith society. Students should take time to reflect on these lessons and how they can apply them in their daily lives.
Class activity:
Students will write one thing they learned this term that they will apply in their life, and share it with the class if they wish.
Evaluation questions:
No formal evaluation during the closing session.
Summary:
This term has helped us understand the early Church and learn important lessons about Christian living that we can apply in our daily lives.
